First Appeal No. 190 of 1996
with
Civil Order No. 13 of 1996
lawyer:
Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim with Mr. Ismail Gazi, Advocates ------- for the appellant. 
Mr. H.R. Nandi with Mr. A.H. Mahfuzur Rahman, Advocates ------- for the respondents.
parties:
Sree Naru Gopal Roy ------- Appellant
Vs.
Parimal Rani Roy and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha, J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.6.96 passed by the 1st Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Jhenidah in Title Suit No.1 of 1996 dismissing the suit for specific performance of a contract. 

 7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned judgment and decree dated 24.5.95, the plaintiff preferred the appeal before this Court. 

 8. Mr. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in dismissing the suit after believing the agreement for sale witnessed by bainapatra Ext. 1 as a genuine transaction. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that defendant No. 1 fraudulently and collusively sold a major portion of the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 for depriving the plaintiff of his valuable right in the suit property with knowledge of the agreement for sale, the learned Subordinate Judge was clearly wrong in not decreeing the suit, at least in respect of the balance of the suit property measuring 4 decimals. The learned Advocate further submits that the provision of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act providing for refusal to decree a suit for specific performance of a contract on the ground of hardship to the defendant being conspicuously absent in the present case, the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in not decreeing the suit. 

 18. D.W. 2 Sudhir Kumar, who deposed on behalf of all the defendants, stated in his evidence that on the basis of a compromise decree in Title Suit No. 3 of 1980 Ganesh acquired 7 ½  decimals of the suit land standing in the name of his wife Parul Rani Roy. He stated that the plaint, vokalatnama and the compromise petition contain the signatures of Ganesh. He further stated that he is the nephew of Ganesh and lives in the house of his mama for the last 8 years. He stated that on or about 24.5.95 Ganesh was seriously ill and he was not in a position to move and to execute the alleged bainapatra. He stated that defendant No. 1 sold to him 10 ½  decimals of the suit land. He further stated that she also sold 2 ½  decimals of the suit land defendant No. 3 on receiving proper consideration and they have house in the purchased land. He stated that the plaintiff's story of agreement for sale is false. He further stated that the alleged bainapatra is false and fabricated and it was never executed by Ganesh. He also stated that the story of receiving subsequent consideration money by Ganesh is false and concocted. He stated that he never knew about the alleged bainapatra before his purchase. He stated that defendant No. 1 sold some property to him and to defendant No. 3 on legal necessities. 19. D.W.3 Parimal Rani Roy as defendant No. I stated in her evidence that her husband Ganesh never entered into an agreement for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff and he never received any money from the plaintiff on executing any bainapatra. She stated that she had sold a portion of the suit property on legal necessities. In cross-examination she stated that she is not a relation of the plaintiff. She asserted that her husband never executed the alleged bainapatra. 

 22. From the scrutiny of the evidence discussed above, we find that the disputed bainapatra dated 24.5.95 Ext. 1 has been convincingly proved by P.Ws. 1, 2, 3 and 5, of which P.W.2 Gour Mohan and P.W.3 Majibur are attesting witnesses and P.W.5 Mohiuddin is the scribe. All these witnesses uniformly stated in their evidence that Gnash executed the bainapatra Ext. 1 in their presence on receiving Tk. 3,00,001.00 as earnest money. The defence has totally failed to shaken their consistent and corroborative testimony in any manner whatsoever. The learned Subordinate Judge took the pains of comparing the disposed signature of under Ganesh appearing in the bainapatra Ext. 1 with his admitted signatures in the plaint and the compromise petition filed in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998 and found that the signatures of Ganesh appearing in the disputed bainapatra Ext 1 tally with his disputed signatures appearing in the plaint and the compromise petition filed in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998. 

 23. Section 73 of the Evidence Act clearly empowers the court to do it. The learned Sub-ordinance Judge, therefore, committed no mistake in not sending the disputed signatures of Ganesh appearing in the bainapatra Ext 1 for comparing and examining the same by a hand writing expert with his admitted signatures in the plaint and the compromise petition filed in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998. We have also carefully compared the signatures of Ganesh appearing in the bainapatra Ext 1 with his admitted signatures in the plaint and the compromise petition filed in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998. We are satisfied that these are the produceds of the same hand. We, are, therefore, inclined to find that the learned Subordinate Judge was fully justified in holding that Ganesh duly executed the bainapatra dated 24.5.95 Ext. 1 on receipt of earnest money amounting to Tk. 3,00,001.00 from the plaintiff. Except denying the genuineness of the bainapatra in question, the defendants produced nothing before the Court to discard the corroborative and consistent evidence of competent witnesses proving bainapatra Ext. 1. We, therefore, find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the defendant respondents that the learned trial Court committed error of law in replying on the unregistered bainapatra without taking necessary assistance from a hand writing expert. 

 24. It has been consistently held by this court that the art of calligraphy is yet to attain any degree of precision so that the Court can place explicit reliance on it. The Court being the expert of the experts was itself quite competent to compare the disputed signatures of Ganesh appearing in the disputed bainapatra Ext 1 with his admitted signatures appearing in the plaint and the compromise petition of Title Suit No. 13 of 1998 and rightly found that the disputed signatures appearing in bainapatra Ext I are of Ganesh. In the facts of the case and the evidence on record, we have no hesitation in affirming, the said finding of fact arrived at by the learned trial Court on sound and cogent reasons that the bainapatra Ext I was duly executed by Ganesh on receiving earnest money amounting to Tk. 3,00,000.00 promising to execute and register a sale deed in respect of the suit property within 6 months on receipt of the balance of the consideration money. In the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, we are inclined to hold that the fact of agreement for sale of the suit property by Ganesh to the plaintiff was within the full knowledge of defendant No. 1 Parimal Rani Roy. It has also been consistently stated by the P.Ws. that after the death of Ganesh, the plaintiff approached defendant No. 1 for execution and registration of the promised kabala on receipt of the balance of the consideration but she consumed time on some plea or the other. Thereafter defendant No. 1, with oblique motives, should away to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by 2 kabalas dated 12.8.95 Ext. H & I for a huge amount of money in the name of meeting legal necessities. There is no dispute to the fact that defendant No. 1 had only a life interest in the suit property but she sold the major portion of the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in order to frustrate the agreement duly entered into by Ganesh. It is unfortunate that the plaintiff has made out no case either in the plaint or in the evidence that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 are subsequent purchasers of the suit property with notice and knowledge of Ganesh's existing contract for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff so as to bind them by the contract in question. Although the conduct of the defendants appears to be shady, we are not in opposition to haul up defendant Nos. 2 and 3, in the absence of a specific case made out by the plaintiff within the ambit of section 27 of the Specific Relief Act, so as to make the subsequent transferees defendant Nos. 2 and 3 bound by the subsisting contract. 

 25. It is found from the evidence on record that Ganesh left no other property except the suit land. It is also found that shortly after the death of Ganesh on 30.6.95 defendant No.1 Parimal Rani Roy hurriedly sold away 13 ½  decimals of the suit land to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 at a consideration of Tk. 2,48,000.00, much above the shown requirement for meeting the alleged legal necessities. It was indeed a fraudulent move to deny the plaintiff of his right arising out of the agreement duly entered into by Ganesh for the sale of the suit property to the plaintiff. It is, of course, true that the plaintiff has not been able to adduce any cogent and reliable evidence to prove that Ganesh subsequently received Tk. 2,48,000.00 by installments by making endorsements therefore on the back of the bainapatra. We are, therefore, of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any mistake in not accepting the subsequent payments by the plaintiff to Ganesh. However, in view of the fact that Ganesh duly entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the suit property at a total consideration of Tk. 5,50,00.00 and duly received Tk. 3,00,001.00 from the plaintiff as earnest money and executed the bainapatra dated 24.5.95 Ext. 1, the plaintiff has the right to pray for specific performance of the contract. With only limited interest in the suit property, defendant No. 1 Parul Rani fraudulently and collusively sold most part of the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 at a huge amount of money amounting to Tk. 2,80,000.00 shortly after the death of Ganesh and this clearly proves that defendant No. 1 did not dispose of most part of the suit property for legal necessities. Since it is not a suit for declaration that the sale deeds obtained by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 from defendant No. 1 Parul Rani are not for legal necessities and these are illegal, collusive and void and no case having been made out by the plaintiff that the subsequent purchasers defendant Nos. 2 and 3 purchased a major portion of the suit land from defendant No. 1 with notice or knowledge of the plaintiffs contract for sale, we are not in a position to declare the subsequent sales void or invalid. But the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the relief under the Specific Relief Act being a equitable relief, a decree for specific performance of the contract with regard to the remaining portion of the suit property excluding the land sold to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 vide Exts I & H cannot be allowed to stand on the ground of hardship to defendant No.1. We have already found that defendant No. 1 did not bonafide sell the major portion of the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 for legal necessities. The sale of most part of the suit property at a consideration of Tk. 2,48,000.00 does not prove any legal necessity to justify the sale. It is thus evident that defendant No. 1 disposed of most part of the suit property with the clear object of depriving the plaintiff of his valuable right arising out of a solemn contract duly entered into by deceased Ganesh. In the facts of the case and the evidence on record, the plea of hardship on the part of defendant No. 1 or her successors as a defence against a decree for specific performance of the contract stands disproved. We are, therefore, unable to accept the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree for specific performance of the contract in respect of the remaining decimals of the suit property, excluding the land covered by Kablas Ext I and H obtained by defendant Nos. 2 and 3, on the ground of hardship, which stands negative by the evidence on record. 

 26. The age old maxim that he who seeks equity must do equity himself applies in full force in the present case. In the facts of the case and the evidence on record, we are of the view that defendant Nos. 1 never acted bonafide in selling most part of the suit property to defendant Nos. 2 and 3 but she consciously did so aiming at frustrating her husband's agreement for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff. In such circumstances, we do not find any difficulty in decreeing the suit in part in respect of 4 decimals of the suit property, after excluding 13 ½ decimals of land covered by exts. I and H. The plaintiff though entitled under the law to get proportionate refund of the earnest money, a money decree against the reversationers of Ganesh, who are admittedly permanent residents of India and who have no legal obligation under the agreement in question, a money decree passed against them will be clearly infructuous. It will be in the fitness of things and quite in consonance with the principle of justice, equity and good conscience to decree the suit in part in respect of only 4 (four) decimals of the suit property. The plaintiff must suffer for his own failure to make out a case under section 27 of the Specific Relief Act, although there were sufficient materials on record to do so. 

 27. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part and the judgment and decree dated 30.6.96 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Jhenaidah dismissing Title Suit No. 13 of 1989 are set aside. Title Suit No. 13 of 1989 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Jhenaidah is decreed in part in respect of only 4 (four) decimals of the suit property. Respondent No. 1(1) Bishu, Bipul and Bijan as the substituted heirs of Ganesh are directed to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of four (4) decimals of the suit land within 3 months from date, failing which the plaintiff shall be at liberty to get a sale deed executed and registered through the Court in accordance with law. Connected Civil Order No. 14 of 1996 stands discharged.
